title: Fiber to Butyrate
description: Interactive model of the fiber-to-short-chain-fatty-acid pathway. Fiber enters the colon, gut bacteria ferment it into acetate, propionate, and butyrate, and butyrate fuels colon-lining cells and strengthens the tight junction seal. Learners change fiber intake and microbe diversity and watch fermentation, colonocyte fuel, and barrier meters respond. A separate, clearly labeled panel shows microglia and blood-brain barrier findings from germ-free mice only.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: neuroscience (gut-brain axis)
publisher: Gut Check: The Neuroscience of How Your Gut and Brain Talk
learningObjectives: Trace dietary fiber through bacterial fermentation to acetate, propionate, and butyrate, and describe where each one mainly goes in the body.
Explain how butyrate fuels colonocytes and supports the tight junction seal of the gut lining.
Distinguish findings shown in people from brain effects (microglia maturation and blood-brain barrier tightness) shown only in germ-free mice.
prerequisites: Gut microbes live mostly in the colon (Chapter 3)
The gut lining is sealed by tight junctions (Chapter 4)
The blood-brain barrier controls what enters the brain (Chapter 5)
keyQuestions: Why does fiber reach the colon instead of being digested in the small intestine?
Which short-chain fatty acid do colon-lining cells use most as fuel?
How does microbe diversity change what the same amount of fiber produces?
Which effects in the model come only from germ-free mouse studies?
misconceptions: All fiber is the same and does the same thing in the gut.
Butyrate is the most abundant short-chain fatty acid in the blood (acetate usually is).
The gut barrier is either completely sealed or completely leaky.
Because gut microbes tighten the blood-brain barrier in germ-free mice, eating more fiber must do the same in people.
